title: Triśaṅku’s declaration: ‘I am the mover of the tree’
theme: A seer speaks in the first person as one who has reached the goal; the verse is handed on as a text to be recited by the student.

words.context: Śaṅkara: «उच्छेद्यात्मकस्य संसारवृक्षस्य» (the tree of saṃsāra, whose nature is to be felled)

words.gram: m. nom. sg., agent noun from an intensive stem (derivation uncertain)

words.role: marks the comparison: ‘[high] like a mountain’s summit’

words.meaning: he whose purifier is on high
words.context: Śaṅkara: «ऊर्ध्वं कारणं पवित्रं पावनं ज्ञानप्रकाश्यं परं ब्रह्म यस्य»

words.meaning: in the one possessed of food/vigour (the sun)

words.role: verb of the third clause (understood in the next)

words.gram: m. nom. sg., tatpuruṣa (or two words, amṛtaḥ akṣitaḥ)

sandhi.rule: A visarga after a vowel other than a or ā becomes r before a vowel: gireḥ iva → girer iva.
aḥ before the voiced v becomes o (P. 6.1.114 (हशि च), then a + u → o). vājini + iva: i + i → ī, P. 6.1.101 (अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः).
u before a dissimilar vowel becomes v: su + amṛtam → svamṛtam, P. 6.1.77 (इको यणचि).
After ā a visarga is dropped before a vowel, and the hiatus stays.
a + u → o: P. 6.1.87 (आद्गुणः). (On the other reading, amṛtaḥ akṣitaḥ, aḥ + a → o with the a elided, written without avagraha.)
oḥ before a voiced consonant: the visarga becomes r.

samasa.meaning: he whose purifier is on high — for Śaṅkara, he whose cause, the supreme Brahman, is the purifier
sprinkled with the immortal (one of Śaṅkara’s two readings)
the utterance that follows the attainment of knowledge (Śaṅkara)

morphology.note: A rare form with a reduplicated root syllable. Rāmānanda calls it an intensive with the intensive suffix dropped («रेरिवा इति यङ्लुगन्तम्») from a root rī ‘to wear away’ («रीङ्घातुः क्षयार्थः»), hence ‘destroyer’; Śaṅkara glosses ‘mover, impeller’ (prerayitā). The nominative in -ā suggests a stem in -van. The derivation is uncertain and is marked so.
Locative singular of vājin, ‘possessing vāja (food, vigour)’; with iva it fuses to vājinīva. Śaṅkara and Rāmānanda take vājin as the sun, who brings food through rain.
A bahuvrīhi with medhā takes the stem sumedhas, P. 5.4.122 (नित्यमसिच् प्रजामेधयोः); the nominative singular is sumedhāḥ.
Genitive singular of the u-stem triśaṅku: guṇa of the final u + s (triśaṅko-ḥ).
Stated once in the third line and understood with what follows: ‘[I am] radiant wealth, [I am] wise, …’ (Śaṅkara: «अस्मीत्यनुवर्तते»).

translation.literal: I [am] the mover of the tree. [My] fame [is high] like the summit of a mountain. Having the purifier on high, I am the excellent immortal, as in the one possessed of vigour [the sun]. [I am] radiant wealth. [I am] of good understanding, sprinkled with the immortal. Thus [is] Triśaṅku’s utterance after knowledge.
translation.readable: I am the one who shakes the tree. My name stands high as a mountain’s ridge. Made pure from on high, I am the pure immortal, as it shines in the sun. I am treasure, full of light. I am wise, immortal, untouched by decay. — So spoke Triśaṅku when he had come to know.

anvaya: अहम् वृक्षस्य रेरिवा [अस्मि] । [मम] कीर्तिः गिरेः पृष्ठम् इव [उच्छ्रिता] । ऊर्ध्वपवित्रः [अहम्] वाजिनि इव सु अमृतम् अस्मि । द्रविणम् सवर्चसम् [अस्मि] । सुमेधाः अमृतोक्षितः [अस्मि] । इति त्रिशङ्कोः वेदानुवचनम् ।
syntax: Five short first-person statements, mostly without a verb; asmi (‘I am’) appears once, in the third, and is carried to the rest. Two of them are comparisons with iva. The last line, in the third person, labels the whole as a quotation: ‘thus [is] Triśaṅku’s veda-anuvacana’.

ambiguities.topic: What is the ‘tree’, and what does rerivā do to it?
ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara: the tree of saṃsāra, which is to be felled, and rerivā is its mover — the speaker, having become Brahman, moves it as its inner controller («अन्तर्याम्यात्मना»). Rāmānanda and Kūranārāyaṇa: its destroyer («भृशं क्षपयिता», Kūranārāyaṇa); the verse Madhva cites says ‘cutter of the tree of saṃsāra’ («संसारवृक्षच्छेत्ताऽहं»). Gopālānanda also allows the body as the tree and the self as its mover. Kūranārāyaṇa reads ahaṃvṛkṣasya as one word: ‘of the great tree of I-making’ («अहङ्कारमहावृक्षस्य»).

Śaṅkara, Rāmānanda and Gopālānanda divide vājini iva su amṛtam: ‘like (the immortal) in the sun, I am the excellent immortal’. The verse Madhva cites reads a name of Viṣṇu in the sun, vājinīvasu («तत्रस्थो भगवान् विष्णुस्सम्प्रोक्तो वाजिनीवसुः»), which divides the same letters differently. Kūranārāyaṇa takes vājinī as the eternal realm («वाजिनी - नित्यविभूतिः» in his gloss).

One compound, ‘sprinkled with the immortal’, or two words, amṛtaḥ akṣitaḥ, ‘immortal, undecaying’. Śaṅkara gives both, the second first («अमृतः अमरणधर्मा अक्षितः अक्षीणः»), and supports the compound with a Brāhmaṇa phrase («अमृतोक्षितोऽहम्»). The base prints no avagraha, so the letters allow either.

For Śaṅkara the speaker speaks as one who has realised identity with Brahman, like Vāmadeva; hence he can call himself the mover of the world-tree. Gopālānanda (modern) insists that the self is like the immortal, not identical with it («न तु तदेवामृतमहम्»).

metre.name: irregular
metre.note: Kūranārāyaṇa calls the verse a six-pāda jagatī («इयं षट्पदा जगति»). As printed the five verse lines count 8, 8, 14, 7 and 8 syllables (45); the third line divides into 9 + 5 at vājinīva, or 8 + 6 if su amṛtam is read uncontracted. A jagatī of six pādas would have 48; the remaining difference is not reconciled here.

beginner: Here a sage named Triśaṅku speaks as someone who has reached the end of the search. He says: I am the one who shakes the tree — the great tree of a life caught in endless coming and going. My name stands as high as a mountain ridge. I am pure, I am deathless like the light in the sun, I am a treasure full of brightness, I am wise and never wasting away. It sounds like boasting, but the tradition hears it differently: it is the voice of someone describing what he discovered about himself, not about his achievements. The passage was kept so that students could recite it, as a reminder of where study is meant to lead.
analogy: Like a climber’s note left in the summit register: brief, a little exultant, and written less for himself than for those still on the slope, to say that the top is real.

commentary.q: What does the passage actually say?
commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: Five short sentences in the first person: I am the rerivā of the tree; my fame is like a mountain’s summit; with my purifier on high, I am the good immortal, as in the vājin; radiant wealth; well-minded, amṛtokṣita. Then a label: ‘thus Triśaṅku’s vedānuvacana’. The text does not say what the tree is, what the speaker had realised, or why the verse is placed here.

commentary.q: Why is this verse placed after the list of duties?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara: it is a text for recitation («स्वाध्यायार्थो मन्त्राम्नायः»), and the recitation serves the arising of knowledge («अस्य च जपो विद्योत्पत्त्यर्थोऽधिगम्यते»). Its place, right after the duties of 1.9, shows that to one who performs the obligatory rites without desire and wishes to know Brahman, seers’ insights about the self appear («एवं श्रौतस्मार्तेषु नित्येषु कर्मसु युक्तस्य निष्कामस्य परं ब्रह्म विविदिषोरार्षाणि दर्शनानि प्रादुर्भवन्त्यात्मादिविषयाणीति»). Kūranārāyaṇa and Gopālānanda agree that it is a mantra to be recited for the success of knowledge («विद्यासमृद्ध्यर्थं जप्तव्यो मन्त्रः»).

commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: veda here is taken not as the scripture but as ‘knowing’: «वेदः वेदनम् आत्मैकत्वविज्ञानम्», and anuvacana as speech that follows (anu) its attainment. Śaṅkara compares Triśaṅku to Vāmadeva, who declared his identity with all things: «वामदेववत्त्रिशङ्कुना आर्षेण दर्शनेन दृष्टो मन्त्राम्नाय आत्मविद्याप्रकाशक इत्यर्थः». Gopālānanda follows him on the word («वेदो वेदनमात्मविज्ञानं तदनुवचनम्»). Kūranārāyaṇa reads vedānuvacana as the speaking of a mantra in meditation, and says the seer is named to show the mantra’s greatness («ऋषिनिर्देशो मन्त्रस्य माहात्म्य सूचनार्थः»).

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The text gives only the name. For Śaṅkara he is a seer who knew Brahman («त्रिशङ्कोः ऋषेः ब्रह्मभूतस्य ब्रह्मविदः»). Kūranārāyaṇa calls him a kṣatriya seer («क्षत्रियमहर्षेः»). The verse Madhva cites from the Yajurviveka calls him a king, a descendant of Manu, and a seer of mantras («इत्याह मन्त्रदृक् पूर्वं त्रिशङ्कुर्मानवो नृपः»). Whether this is the Triśaṅku of the epic stories is not said by any of them.

commentary.q: How can a person say ‘I am the immortal’?
commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: Here the schools part. For Śaṅkara the speaker has realised that the self is the one pure reality; ‘I am the good immortal’ is literally so («एवं सु अमृतं शोभनं विशुद्धमात्मतत्त्वम् अस्मि भवामि»). Rāmānanda reads the verse as the freed self whose true nature has become manifest: free of all change, not part of saṃsāra («सकलभावविकाररहितोऽसंसारीत्यर्थः»). Gopālānanda says the self is like that immortal, not that immortal itself («न तु तदेवामृतमहम्»). The verse Madhva cites makes the purity and immortality gifts of Hari, by whom the speaker is purified and pervaded («अत्युत्कृष्टेन हरिणा पावितोऽस्मि यतः स्फुटम्»).

commentary.q: What does the verse say to a reader now?
commentary.label: reflection
commentary.text: Whatever its doctrine, the verse records a voice that is no longer anxious. It does not ask for anything; it says what is so. Placed after a list of duties and before the teacher’s parting instructions, it reads like a glimpse of the destination given in the middle of the road — a reason to keep going. This is a modern reflection.

advaita.text: The speaker speaks as Brahman, as Vāmadeva did. He moves the tree of saṃsāra as its inner self («अहं वृक्षस्य उच्छेद्यात्मकस्य संसारवृक्षस्य रेरिवा प्रेरयिता अन्तर्याम्यात्मना»); his omniscience is shown in the creation, maintenance and dissolution of the world. The recitation helps knowledge to arise in one who performs the rites without desire.

visistadvaita.text: Kūranārāyaṇa: having cut down the tree of ego, the speaker has reached supreme devotion to Nārāyaṇa («परस्मिन् ब्रह्मणि नारायणे परां भक्तिं प्राप्तः») and enjoys the immortal like the eternally free («नित्यमुक्तवत्परमामृतभोक्तास्मि»). Rāmānanda reads the verse as the freed self’s nature become manifest. Gopālānanda: the self resembles the Supreme by its own pure nature («नैसर्गिकशुद्धस्वभावतस्तत्साधर्म्यात् तत्सदृशोऽहमस्मि»).

dvaita.text: Madhva comments only through verses he cites from a work he calls the Yajurviveka: the speaker is the cutter of the tree, purified by Hari, and immortal because pervaded by Viṣṇu who dwells in the sun, called vājinīvasu («तेनामृतेन सिक्तोहं तेन व्याप्तो यतस्सदा»). The verses are reported as cited by Madhva.

schools.disagreement: All read the verse as the utterance of one who has reached the goal, and all treat it as a text for recitation. They differ on the ‘I’: identical with Brahman (Śaṅkara), the freed self resembling the Supreme and devoted to Nārāyaṇa (Kūranārāyaṇa, Rāmānanda, Gopālānanda), or a self purified and pervaded by Viṣṇu (Madhva’s cited verses).

parallels.note: Śaṅkara compares Triśaṅku to Vāmadeva, who, seeing this, declared ‘I was Manu, and the sun’ — a seer speaking in the first person from knowledge.
The Gītā’s tree of saṃsāra, to be cut with the strong axe of non-attachment — the image the commentators find in ‘the tree’.

contemporary.text: First-person declarations today are usually about achievement: what I built, what I won. Triśaṅku’s ‘I am’ is of a different kind. Read with the commentators, it is not a claim about status but a report of what the self turned out to be when it was no longer defined by its possessions — so that ‘my fame is high as a mountain’ becomes a statement of clarity, not of reputation. The contrast can be a useful test for one’s own self-descriptions. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: If you described yourself without mentioning any job, possession or achievement, what would you say?
reflect.deeper: Why might a tradition hand on a seer’s first-person words to be recited by students who have not yet seen what he saw?
reflect.practice: Write down three sentences beginning ‘I am’ that do not depend on anything you own or have done. Read them again in a week.

references.text: Madhva’s entire comment on this anuvāka consists of verses he cites from the Yajurviveka; Śaṅkara cites a Brāhmaṇa phrase (‘amṛtokṣito ’ham’) in support of one reading of amṛtokṣitaḥ.

flags.note: The derivation of rerivā is uncertain; the commentators derive it differently (Śaṅkara ‘mover’, Rāmānanda an intensive of rī ‘destroyer’).
The metre: Kūranārāyaṇa’s ‘six-pāda jagatī’ is not reconciled with the printed syllable count (45).
Madhva’s cited verse implies the division vājinīvasu for the letters read by the others as vājini iva su; the edition prints the base text’s spacing.
